title: In a head model scaled with human ECoG, stent channels in the superior sagittal sinus record leg and supplementary motor cortex but get less than 1% of their high-gamma signal from the hand area
abstract: Stent-electrode channels in the superior sagittal sinus, the large vein above the brain where Stentrode arrays are implanted, record the leg area and the supplementary motor area (SMA), but they get less than 1% of their high-gamma signal from the hand area. This matters because endovascular and sub-scalp brain-computer interfaces are in human trials, and their designers must choose electrode sites without human data on what each site records. We built a finite-difference volume-conductor model of one adult head (1 mm voxels) with the sinus, its dural wall, a 3 mm fluid gap to the cortex, the falx and the dura. We computed lead fields (the voltage per unit cortical dipole) for 514 electrodes on the sinus wall and, over the sensorimotor cortex, on the scalp, on the skull (sub-scalp), on and under the dura, and on the brain. We scaled the model of high-gamma (70-200 Hz) activity with public subdural ECoG data. A 16-electrode stent over the leg area takes about 60% of its channel power from the leg areas and at most about 0.5% from the hand area. For attempted movement of both ankles the model gives a 36% high-gamma amplitude change (19-45% over the unknown reference electrode, 24-46% over calibration channels); a published Stentrode patient showed 54%. For the 23-55% change reported for attempted hand movement in a second patient, hand-area power would have to rise about 80- to 900-fold (and 22 to 150 times more than calibrated even if that activity were fully coherent), but a rise of leg-area power by about 0.9 times its resting level is sufficient, so this signal very likely comes from cortex near the midline. For a 1 cm2 patch with 1 nAm/mm2, the best sinus electrode records 233 uV from the leg area and 36 uV from the hand area (subdural electrodes: 472 and 638 uV; sub-scalp: 16 and 21 uV). With 0.5 uV noise, a stent detects a doubling of high-gamma power in one 1 cm2 patch over 17 cm2 of medial cortex and 10 mm subdural grids over 89 cm2; sub-scalp grids reach a 10% change only over 1 cm2 at 0.25 uV and 21 cm2 at 0.1 uV. An electrode in a 2 mm cortical vein records like an electrode on the brain surface. Dura conductivity from 0.05 to 1.5 S/m and sinus-cortex gaps from 1.5 to 5 mm do not change these conclusions. Limits: one head at 1 mm resolution, high gamma modelled as random dipoles, absolute predictions uncertain by a factor of about 2, two patients with ALS and unknown stent positions, stent metal not modelled.
